node.label: Kristin L. Hoganson
node.date_label: Fighting for American Manhood (1998) · Consumers’ Imperium (2007) · The Heartland (2019) · Crossing Empires, with Jay Sexton (2020)
node.description: In Fighting for American Manhood (1998), Kristin L. Hoganson argues that ideals of masculine citizenship and political leadership helped propel the United States into the Spanish-American and Philippine-American wars. Consumers’ Imperium (2007) brings empire into the household, showing how affluent white women’s consumption of foreign goods helped form a sense of global entitlement. Christopher Endy praised the latter book’s account of women’s place in globalization, while Mary Renda asked for a more precise chronology and stronger links to political, military and economic events; Mari Yoshihara wanted more attention to the people who shaped consumer choices. In her response, Hoganson defended domestic consumption as a manifestation of empire while acknowledging that she had not established direct links between particular consumer groups and policy decisions. The Heartland (2019) challenges the presumed isolation of the rural Midwest; Crossing Empires (2020), coedited with Jay Sexton, places U.S. history within relations among empires.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Fighting for American Manhood: How Gender Politics Provoked the Spanish-American and Philippine-American Wars (1998); “Cosmopolitan Domesticity: Importing the American Dream, 1865–1920” (2002); Consumers’ Imperium: The Global Production of American Domesticity, 1865–1920 (2007); American Empire at the Turn of the Twentieth Century: A Brief History with Documents (2017); The Heartland: An American History (2019); Crossing Empires: Taking U.S. History into Transimperial Terrain (2020), coedited with Jay Sexton.
node.scope_note: Complete 2020 memoir and its notes read. Selected 2008 roundtable passages, the joint 2020 preface, introduction pp. 1–3 and notes pp. 19–21, and Iacovetta pp. 32–35 and 44 read. Publisher descriptions and publication metadata checked. Monographs, most introduction pages, individual volume chapters and the works named as intellectual debts remain unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: Hoganson’s “Edging In” (2020) credits Cott with supervising her undergraduate thesis and doctorate.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Memoir, paragraphs beginning “These three developments” and “My senior year”; retrospective testimony; theses unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: Hoganson names Rosenberg’s Spreading the American Dream (1982) among her formative foreign-relations texts in “Edging In” (2020).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Memoir, note 5: “influenced me greatly”; specific uptake unspecified.

proposed_edges.relationship: Hoganson names Rodgers’s Atlantic Crossings (1998) among her formative foreign-relations texts in “Edging In” (2020).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Memoir, note 5; specific uptake unspecified; original unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: Hoganson names Kaplan and Donald Pease’s jointly edited Cultures of United States Imperialism (1993) as formative in “Edging In” (2020).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Memoir, note 5; joint editorial credit; collection unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: Hoganson and Jay Sexton's introduction to Crossing Empires (2020) quotes Iriye's 2002 distinction between international and transnational history, then argues that the transnational frame does not fully capture, and can obscure, the imperial relations behind cross-border links.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Joint introduction pp. 2–3: Iriye’s definition frames the cable example; the next paragraph says transnational “does not fully capture” its relations. Their argument is jointly authored. Iriye’s original 2002 essay and the rest of the introduction are unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: Fighting for American Manhood (1998) explains U.S. war and imperial politics through gendered citizenship, political leadership and the prestige attached to martial manhood.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Yale publisher description, paragraphs 1–4, explicitly joins gender and international relations history and identifies politicians’ use of manhood and soldier-citizenship ideals. Illinois confirms original 1998; Yale lists later editions. Description read; full book unread.
proposed_edges.map_label: Masculinity in war and imperial politics

proposed_edges.relationship: Consumers’ Imperium (2007) makes affluent white women’s imported furnishings, dress, food and leisure practices part of the history of U.S. global power.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: UNC Press description, paragraphs 1–4, moves from exports and production to imports and household demand. Its scope is predominantly well-to-do white women; no universal consumer experience asserted. Publisher page read; full book unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: Hoganson and Jay Sexton’s Crossing Empires introduction (2020) argues that histories of cross-border connection must identify the imperial power relations that enabled them.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Joint introduction pp. 1–3, especially cable communications as both cross-border networks and imperial routes/materials. “call out empire” states the program. Selected pages and publisher description read; contributors’ individual arguments and complete volume unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: Fighting for American Manhood (1998) contributes to military history by explaining how politicians’ anxieties about national manliness encouraged the Spanish-American and Philippine-American wars.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read Fraser’s substantive military-history discussion and note 83 in the journal’s open text. Fraser identifies Hoganson’s use of congressional debates as an example of historical analysis of martial masculinity. This establishes a field contribution, not personal influence on Fraser or on the historians discussed alongside her. Hoganson’s book was not read for this proposal.

proposed_edges.relationship: The Heartland: An American History (2019) recasts Midwestern history through settler colonialism and colonial dispossession, placing the United States within comparative settler-colonial historiography.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read Bradley’s introduction and the reviews. The claim concerns Hoganson’s historiographical framing; the book itself remains unread. No community narratives or knowledge are reproduced.

proposed_edges.relationship: The Heartland: An American History (2019) connects Midwestern agricultural and environmental history with imperial networks, including the international circulation of livestock.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Bradley explicitly identifies environmental history; Merleaux develops the agricultural examples. This is a field contribution supported by reviews, not evidence of personal intellectual debt.
